person.name: Lydia E Norwood
person.notes:
Lydia E. Clark (born Lydia Norwood) was a prominent 19th-century Nanticoke Indian elder from Delaware, historically regarded as the last fluent speaker of the Nanticoke language. Born in the late 1700s, she lived much of her life in Indian River Hu | ndred, Sussex County, where she maintained traditional Indian customs. | The 1855 Court Trial | Lydia Clark is most frequently remembered for her decisive role as an expert witness in an 1855 racial trial in Millsboro, Delaware. | The Conflict: A successful Nanticoke businessman, Levin Sockum, was accused of violating a law that prohibited selling gunpowder to "Negroes" or "mulattoes" after he sold ammunition to his cousin, Isaiah (Isaac) Harmon. Both me | n identified as Nanticoke Indians. | Testimony: At age 87, Clark testified that the community was descended from a legendary union between an Irish woman (sometimes named Regua) and an enslaved African prince (or "Congo chief") who had intermarried with local Nanticokes befo | re the American Revolution. | Outcome: Based largely on her testimony, an all-white jury determined that Sockum and Harmon were "Negro" or "mulatto," effectively erasing their legal status as Indians at that time. | Controversy and Coerced Testimony | The Nanticoke Indian Association and modern historians have challenged the accuracy of her 1855 testimony, maintainng an oral tradition that it was coerced. | Dependency: In her old age, Clark was infirm and lived on the land of a white landowner, Nathaniel Burton, on whom she was entirely dependent. | Repentance: According to one of her descendants, she died repentant, allegedly telling relatives that she had "dishonored her people" through her forced testimony. | Identity and Heritage | Physical Appearance: Contemporaries, including the prosecutor George Fisher, described Clark as a "perfect Indian type" with "perfect Caucasian features" and "copper-colored" skin. | Family Ties: She was the sister of "Noke" (Noble) Norwood, a leader in the Indian community. Her grandson, William Russell Clark (also known as Chief Wyniaco), served as the leader of the Nanticoke Indian Association from 1880 until 1928. | Tribal Title: The Nanticoke Indian Association respectfully refers to her as "Princess Nau-Gau-Okwa". | Death and Legacy | Lydia Clark died on December 26, 1856. | The "Last Indian" Fallacy: Her gravestone, erected in 1927 in a dense pine forest in Indian River Hundred, bears the inscription: "The last one of the Aborigines of the country". However, tribal members and historians note thi | s is a fallacy, as the Nanticoke community she was part of continues to thrive today. | Language Revival: While the Nanticoke language was considered extinct following her death, a revival effort began in 2007 using vocabulary lists previously compiled by figures like Thomas Jefferson. | Monuments: In addition to her grave, there is a large stone monument to her at Riverdale Park erected by the Colonial Dames of Delaware, though it erroneously lists her death year as 1859. | Lydia Norwood 1790-1856 | Lydia E. Clark (born Lydia Norwood, 1790–1856) was a prominent Nanticoke Indian elder from Sussex County, Delaware, historically recognized as the last fluent speaker of the Nanticoke language. Her death on December 26, 1856, was traditionally view | ed as the moment the Nanticoke language became extinct, though revival efforts began in the 21st century. | Family and Community Status | Lydia was a member of the core Nanticoke families in Indian River Hundred. She was the sister of "Noke" (Noble) Norwood, a tall, "copper-colored" man described as a leader in the local Indian community. Her grandson, William Rus | sell Clark (also known as Chief Wyniaco), served as the leader of the Nanticoke Indian Association from 1880 until 1928. Within the tribe, she is respectfully referred to by the title "Princess Nau-Gau-Okwa". | The 1855 Racial Trial | Lydia Clark is most famously known for her role as an "expert witness" in a 1855 racial trial in Millsboro. | The Conflict: Levin Sockum, a successful Nanticoke store owner, was charged with violating a law that prohibited selling gunpowder to "Negroes" or "mulattoes" after he sold ammunition to his cousin, Isaiah (Isaac) Harmon. | Expert Testimony: At age 87, Clark was called to testify because she was universally regarded as an authentic Nanticoke. Contemporaries, including the prosecutor George Fisher, described her as a "perfect Indian type" with a sharp intelli | gence. | The Origin Legend: She testified that the community (often called "Moors") was descended from a union between an Irish woman (sometimes called Regua) and an enslaved African prince (or "Congo chief") who had intermarried with th | e Nanticoke before the American Revolution. | Legal Impact: Based largely on her testimony, an all-white jury determined Harmon and Sockum were "Negro" or "mulatto," effectively stripping them of their legal standing as Indians at that time. | Controversy and Coerced Testimony | Modern historians and the Nanticoke Indian Association maintain that Clark's 1855 testimony was coerced. | Dependency: At the time of the trial, Clark was elderly, infirm, and lived on land owned by a white landowner, Nathaniel Burton, upon whom she was entirely dependent. | Repentance: According to oral tradition passed down through her descendants, Clark died repentant, allegedly telling relatives that she had "dishonored her people" through her forced statements. | Death and Memorials | Lydia Clark died roughly a year after the trial. | The "Last Indian" Monument: In 1927, a large stone monument was erected in her honor in a dense pine forest in Indian River Hundred (near Riverdale Park). | The Inscription: The stone bears a controversial inscription calling her: "The last one of the Aborigines of the country... a witness against the arrogant negros that assumed to be what they were not". | Legacy: Tribal members and historians have long pointed out the fallacy of the "Last Indian" label, as the Nanticoke community she was part of remains a thriving reality in Delaware and New Jersey today. Another monument at Riverdale Park | , erected by the Colonial Dames of Delaware, erroneously lists her death year as 1859. | </line></notexml></notexml>
[Correction, obituary-dates package 2026-11-27: birth year corrected to abt 1790 on the 1850 census (Indian River Hundred, dwelling 32), which gives Lydia Clark's age as 60, with Mary C. Clark, 20, in her household. The former abt 1768 (the age-87 account of the 1855 Georgetown trial) and the gravestone's implied abt 1781 ('about 75 years' at her 1856 death) stand as conflicting accounts, recorded here, not as equals: a 22-year gap is beyond ordinary census age error. Analysis filed 2026-11-23.]
